Is South Africa going Hungry?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The cost of food is said to rise up to 30% by April next year. With the price of staples and meat soaring, how are ordinary South Africans going to cope when a trip to the shops becomes unaffordable?

Summary:
We are living in very uncertain times, but of all the challenges that currently face us in South Africa, the rising cost of food is one of the biggest. Due to a perfect storm of factors (including severe drought, unstable exchange rate, and a fragile agricultural sector), the price of all our major food products has been rocketing. Until recently, price increases have been largely absorbed by the retailers, but this is about to end and consumers are sure to get an extreme case of ‘sticker shock’.

This will have an impact on all South Africans – but it will be a disproportionately heavy burden for the poor who already spend most of their income of food. In other foods, the issue of food security is a ticking time bomb that could engulf the country in a wave of hunger, social unrest, and even rebellion.

In this incisive piece, we will investigate the issues affecting the rising price of food in South Africa; shedding light on what’s to come and how to prepare for the worst, through the use of personal narratives of ordinary middle class South Africans, ranging to the very poor, expert opinions and graphic treatments.

Further information:
The story begins, appropriately enough, in a supermarket where we will ask ordinary middle class people about the price of food and how they are coping with the rising cost of their shopping trolley.

We will then meet the first of our case studies: the Mazibuko family. They are a middle class couple earning a combined income of around R45 000 a month. They have kids and a number of dependents, such as parents, widowed siblings and other relatives who all need support. The Mazibukos are already stretched thin, but with food prices increasing, that narrow margin will soon be eroded – leaving them (and all their dependants) in dire straits.

A second case study is the Mazibuko’s domestic servant, who earns an average monthly salary of around R6000. Her experiences will serve to underline the fact that food increases will disproportionately affect low income individuals, who are already struggling to survive.

Scenes with the Mazibukos and the domestic worker will be intercut with several interviews, to provide context and opinion. These expert interviews will include representatives from PACSA – who generate a regular ‘food basket’ barometer – to talk about how food costs are calculated and the general implications of a rising food baskets in the future.

To provide the bigger picture, economic strategist, Thabi Leoka will be on hand to discuss the issue of the exchange rate and how it is affecting the cost of food imports (which are necessary because our farms are not able to produce enough to feed the nation), as well as how increasing food prices impact on monthly incomes.

A representative from the Wheat Growers Association, Wandile Shiloobo will be on hand to discuss the impact of the drought and the reality of farmers who are struggling with many challenges, including lack of government subsidies and support.

Finally, we will look at some mitigation strategies that could be implemented – either by the country’s leadership or through individual initiative. For example, some residents of suburban Parkhurst are turning their pavements into vegetable gardens. Other legislative or welfare strategies could also be relevant.

To conclude, our case studies and experts will give us their forecasts for the next few years – when food price increases really begin to bite and the societal backlash becomes more pronounced.

One thing is for sure – an increase in food prices is not an abstract concept. It affects everyone directly, every time they go into the shops. When such a primal physical need is threatened by unaffordable pricing, the foundations of our society may be threatened.

Press Release:


Is SA Going Hungry?
The cost of food could rise by a whopping 30% in the next year. Due to severe drought and an unstable exchange rate, the price of all essential products has been steadily escalating. So far, these increases have largely been absorbed by retailers, but consumers are advised to brace themselves for tough times at the tills. How will ordinary South Africans cope when a trip to the supermarket becomes unaffordable?


Script:


Vox Pops
Claire: When last did you see somebody push a trolley full of groceries?
Vox: (laughs) I don’t know when
Claire: What have you noticed has now become quite expensive
Vox: I think meat in particular
Vox: R19 for a head of brocolli
Vox: 498.47 for this… this is nothing
Claire: aaaah this is painful
Vox: Ja, very painful
Vox: Everything is high like from clothes, transport, food… let’s say living in SA now it’s very very expensive
Link Intro - 30%
Link: Food - it’s a basic human need for survival. South Africans are in for a shock because food prices are projected to rise by up to 30% by next year. How are we going to cope when a trip to the shops becomes simply unaffordable?
Possible Thabi support 30%
Thabi: Basically food prices and even the CPI, so the consumer price index is exactly how it was when we were in a financial crisis.

VO: Economic strategist, Thabi Leoka says South Africans are going to have to tighten their belts considerably over the next few years.

Thabi: We're complaining now and we’re seeing food prices increasing now, but we actually haven’t even felt the full impact of it
5 second montage break of aisles, food costs


Thabi: all along retailers have not really been passing through the cost of products, the real cost of products to consumers
Claire: So they’ve been absorbing those costs?
Thabi: So you absorb the costs and they can do it especially the bigger retailers because they've got a lot of other products that they sell. But there comes a time where they can’t absorb the costs anymore and so they have to now pass it through to consumers.
3 second intro - show Diepsloot and surrounds into Doris cooking, feeding her boy
VO: Many South Africans like Doris NomPumelelo, who is a sole breadwinner and supports a family of four, are finding it harder and harder to put food on the table. As a part time worker, Doris supplements her income by selling sweets at her SPAZA.

Claire Mawisa: Mama what do you do for work and how much do you earn per month?
Doris: Domestic worker, I make R2000 a month, with that R2000 I buy food, pay transport for the kids, pay for my transport. There’s also grant for one child. its R320, I pay preschool with it.
Doris - her lifestyle


Claire: How much money do you spend every month on food?
Doris: I spend maybe about R900 because I look out for the specials

VO: Doris relies on the extra monthly food packages she gets from her church, otherwise her family would be going a lot hungrier.

Doris: It's tin stuff, veggies, mealie meal, tea and sugar.
Mervyn and his trolley
VO: Mervyn Abrahams is the director of PACSA, a social justice organisation based in Pietermaritzburg, which studies the fluctuations in food prices. The PACSA food price Barometer is based on a food basket which consists of thirty-six food products, and on what a low income household of 7 buys monthly
visuals of Doris, Diepsloot
Beat with till items being swiped through
Mervyn: That provides us with a proxy of how the South African economy is in fact doing if we can see whether households in fact do have the means to procure sufficient and nutritious food.
graph in the PACSA document

GRAPHIC:
onions (116%), potatoes (102%), spinach (82%), cooking oil (28%), rice (20%)
VO: Mervyn reports that over the past few years there has been a steady increase in the price of the basket with a massive spike starting in November 2015 of approximately 14%. Some food items increased dramatically, and over the last year maize has increased by 33%.

Mervyn: If we look January to February of this year we saw the basket increasing from well over R1700 to well over R1800.

VO: This PACSA costing is for the less nutritional basket, and considering the median income for a black South African household is R2800 a month, this would leave a family with less than R1000 a month to cover other household expenses.

Doris: I'm struggling because sometimes I go shopping with R1000 and can only afford two bags of groceries so I feel bad because prices are high.

Mervyn: When we look at the cost of a nutritional basket for a household of seven we are closer to four thousand rand and so we can already begin to see the nutritional gap in households.
Bread graphic
VO: Many factors contribute to these spiralling food costs. If one looks at a loaf of bread, wheat is only 20% of the price while 80% accounts for: other ingredients, electricity, water, labour costs, packaging, transport and retailers costs.

Wandile Sihlobo from Grain SA says that the severe drought South Africans have experienced over the last harvesting season, is not the only factor that is contributing to a rise in food prices.

10.5 million tons consumption
7 million tons produced
3.5 million tons shortfall
Wandile: Now that you have drought it means that now South Africa doesn’t have the total grain that we used to consume for example, maize, we consume 10.5 million tons, now you're producing 7 you need to buy something from outside.

VO: With a weak exchange rate, importing food in dollars negatively impacts the overall food processing chain, and ultimately the economy. Even if the rainfall does increase in October, farmers may be unable to recover their deficit. Two key increases in the CPI are food and fuel.
Thabi - rand-dollar
Thabi: Transport is a big part of manufacturing or farmers’ costs. We are also seeing increases in electricity prices of about 9.4%. And so this is why when you hear a 30% increase in food prices next year they’re factoring in also the lag in food prices and also obviously what their projections are for the currency in 2017

VO: With inflation sitting at 7% South Africans are already feeling the squeeze in their daily lives.

Link: Rising food prices have put pressure on all sectors of society, nobody is exempt from having to face the fact that they might have to adjust their lifestyle.

VO: Hardest hit are the rural areas as they don’t have the advantage of urban infrastructure and competitive retailers. But even city professionals, like attorney and mother of four Sandra Miller, are rapidly learning to adapt.
Kitchen - Claire and Sandra chat about challenges
Claire Mawisa: and boys eat a lot!
Sandra: Oh they eat a lot!
Sandra: For mothers food is the most important thing then housing of course.

VO: Together with a group of friends, Sandra created a bargain hunting group where they pool their money.

Sandra: We scout the shops, for example, last week pasta was on special at woolies, it was four for R20, so we quickly went there and we bought in bulk

Sandra: You see mama takes the last one, the smallest one.
Visuals of Doris, township
Mervyn: Mothers love their children so much that they feed their children first and eat last and often there is very little left by the time the mother gets to the pot of food.

Claire Mawisa: What have you stopped buying because it's just too expensive?
Doris: Corn Flakes!
Doris: And I tell my kids, maybe we eat meat 2 times a week because I have no money for the meat.

Sandra: My philosophy is that if you can feed the children then you don’t spend much money with the doctor.

Mervyn: We all know that with less nutrition and on a hungry stomach no child can study, so the investment that is being made in education in fact does not find fertile ground.
Link - innovation, kerbside gardens
Link: In times of crisis we need to start thinking of innovotative solutions like this vegetable garden that's being grown right on the side of the street, not just to benefit individuals but the community at large.

Claire: We feel this is about sharing and about being conscious about food about our effect on our neighborhoods and on the earth.

VO: Claire Reid has developed the “garden in a box” concept to make it easy for anyone to grow their own vegetables

Claire: So the seeds are already in here at correct distance apart with all of the nutrients your plant needs.

Claire Reid: We need to activate people to be able to grow in whatever small space they have available.

VO: Sandra is already ahead of the game, and has cultivated an impressive vegetable garden at home.
Sandra - cutbacks = domestic help & luxuries
Sandra: I've got a little garden at the back there and just in this one in the house there. I've got butternut and spinach, morogo pumpkin, even the pumpkin leaves, you can eat it.
Claire Mawisa: What comprimises in your lifestyle have you had to make, what has had to change in your life?
Sandra: I had to stop the cleaning lady from coming and I also had stop the gardener from coming. So my boys and myself we now clean our house and we do the garden.
Eggs!!!
Mervyn: Household expenditure such as bond repayments, servicing debt, municipal service payments, those payments have to be made every single month. Food then is purchased with the amount of money that households have left over.

VO: And with the looming threat of downgrade to junk status, economists warn the country may face a recession.

Wandile: It's a chicken and egg situation, because you don’t have the jobs and then now the food prices are starting to actually go up - nowhere to work, there’s no food so its a very pretty much challenging situation.
Link - reality check
Link: So maybe the next time you make a trip to the shops you'll grab a basket instead of a trolley because the reality check will hit you at the till.
Closing soundbites
Claire: Have you decided to adjust your lifestyle in any way to accommodate the rising prices...?
Vox: I’ve got no option but to adjust
Vox: I’m like not so brand conscious anymore, I buy by the price
Vox: We don’t eat chocolates like back in the days where you used eat chocolates in the evening, you eat maybe once a month
Vox: The only thing that I’ve done is to reduce the amount of food that I buy, and try and manage that more wisely this time, less wastage
Sandra: Change with the change. Things have changed so you've got to change and I think thats where wisdom comes in.







PROMO 15”:

South Africans are experiencing the pressure of rising food costs daily, shopping for a bargain is becoming a necessity.
VOX POP of Lady with her trolley showing till slip bite: or the bite where someone says “I don’t look for brands anymore … blah blah


PROMO 15”:

Severe drought and an unstable exchange rate has seen the price of all essential products steadily escalate. So far, these increases have largely been absorbed by retailers, but consumers are advised to brace themselves for tough times at the tills.


PROMO 10”:

Food - a basic human need is coming under threat, with costs predicted to rise by 30% next year. Are South Africans going to go hungry?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The cost of food is said to rise up to 30% by April next year. With the price of staples and meat soaring, how are ordinary South Africans going to cope when a trip to the shops becomes unaffordable?
metadata.Summary: We are living in very uncertain times, but of all the challenges that currently face us in South Africa, the rising cost of food is one of the biggest. Due to a perfect storm of factors (including severe drought, unstable exchange rate, and a fragile agricultural sector), the price of all our major food products has been rocketing. Until recently, price increases have been largely absorbed by the retailers, but this is about to end and consumers are sure to get an extreme case of ‘sticker shock’. This will have an impact on all South Africans – but it will be a disproportionately heavy burden for the poor who already spend most of their income of food. In other foods, the issue of food security is a ticking time bomb that could engulf the country in a wave of hunger, social unrest, and even rebellion. In this incisive piece, we will investigate the issues affecting the rising price of food in South Africa; shedding light on what’s to come and how to prepare for the worst, through the use of personal narratives of ordinary middle class South Africans, ranging to the very poor, expert opinions and graphic treatments.
metadata.Further information: The story begins, appropriately enough, in a supermarket where we will ask ordinary middle class people about the price of food and how they are coping with the rising cost of their shopping trolley. We will then meet the first of our case studies: the Mazibuko family. They are a middle class couple earning a combined income of around R45 000 a month. They have kids and a number of dependents, such as parents, widowed siblings and other relatives who all need support. The Mazibukos are already stretched thin, but with food prices increasing, that narrow margin will soon be eroded – leaving them (and all their dependants) in dire straits. A second case study is the Mazibuko’s domestic servant, who earns an average monthly salary of around R6000. Her experiences will serve to underline the fact that food increases will disproportionately affect low income individuals, who are already struggling to survive. Scenes with the Mazibukos and the domestic worker will be intercut with several interviews, to provide context and opinion. These expert interviews will include representatives from PACSA – who generate a regular ‘food basket’ barometer – to talk about how food costs are calculated and the general implications of a rising food baskets in the future. To provide the bigger picture, economic strategist, Thabi Leoka will be on hand to discuss the issue of the exchange rate and how it is affecting the cost of food imports (which are necessary because our farms are not able to produce enough to feed the nation), as well as how increasing food prices impact on monthly incomes. A representative from the Wheat Growers Association, Wandile Shiloobo will be on hand to discuss the impact of the drought and the reality of farmers who are struggling with many challenges, including lack of government subsidies and support. Finally, we will look at some mitigation strategies that could be implemented – either by the country’s leadership or through individual initiative. For example, some residents of suburban Parkhurst are turning their pavements into vegetable gardens. Other legislative or welfare strategies could also be relevant. To conclude, our case studies and experts will give us their forecasts for the next few years – when food price increases really begin to bite and the societal backlash becomes more pronounced. One thing is for sure – an increase in food prices is not an abstract concept. It affects everyone directly, every time they go into the shops. When such a primal physical need is threatened by unaffordable pricing, the foundations of our society may be threatened.
